title: Short Stuff: Straitjackets
summary: Short Stuff episode on straitjackets. Josh and Chuck discuss the origin of the straitjacket in the Georgian period (around 1700s) as a restraint for people with severe mental illness, its link to the growth of asylums in the 17th and 18th centuries, and its decline. They cover King George III and his physician Francis Willis, Houdini's escape stunts (with his brother Theodore Hardeen), the 1829 Lincoln Asylum strangulation death and the asylum's ban on straitjackets, and modern alternatives such as chemical restraint and low-sensory, non-confrontational de-escalation. They discuss Humane Restraint, a Wisconsin company that makes restraints and suicide smocks and sells straitjackets mostly to jails and prisons, and close with music-world straitjacket uses (Alice Cooper, Johnny Rotten in the Sex Pistols' "God Save the Queen" video) and Ludacris's Falcons stunt.

segments.title: Opening banter and what straitjackets are
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic, which Chuck wondered about after seeing straitjackets in TV and movies. Josh describes how straitjackets were used to restrain arms with long sleeves tied behind the back, and the origin of the word 'straight'.

segments.title: Word 'straight' and off-topic banter
segments.summary: The hosts clarify that 'straight' means tightly fitting, not straight and narrow, then joke about Ludacris's Atlanta restaurant and a Falcons game stunt where he descended in a straitjacket.

segments.title: Asylums, King George III and the decline of straitjackets
segments.summary: Straitjacket use rose with the growth of asylums in the 17th and 18th centuries and was justified as more humane than chaining. Josh describes King George III, confined in a straitjacket by his doctor Francis Willis, possibly due to porphyria; his apparent cure marked the start of the idea that mental illness could be cured and the decline of straitjackets. Chuck recommends the film The Madness of King George.

segments.title: Houdini and the straitjacket escape
segments.summary: Chuck notes Houdini used the straitjacket as a stunt performed in view of the audience, and that his brother Theodore Hardeen may have used it first. The hosts mention an earlier Houdini episode.

segments.title: Dangers of straitjackets and modern alternatives
segments.summary: Chuck says straitjackets are outdated; in 1829 a patient at Lincoln Asylum strangled themselves with one, and the asylum banned them. Josh describes modern practice in the United States: physical restraints as a last resort, chemical restraint by injection, and non-confrontational de-escalation in a low-sensory environment.

segments.title: Straitjackets in pop culture
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss how movies and TV keep using the straitjacket as a shorthand for danger, long after it fell out of use. Josh says the media has misinformed people about mental illness.
topics: straitjacket trope in film and TV

segments.title: Humane Restraint company and the prison market
segments.summary: Chuck describes Humane Restraint, a company in Wanaki, Wisconsin, that makes bed restraints, safe furniture, suicide smocks made of moving blanket material, and Humane jackets for about $225, selling fewer than 100 a year, all to jails and prisons. Josh cites a 2014 Treatment Advocacy Center finding that jails and prisons hold far more seriously mentally ill people than state psychiatric hospitals, linking this to the closure of state hospitals. Chuck notes jails are not bound by the same humane-treatment rules.

segments.title: Straitjackets in music and pop culture
segments.summary: The hosts discuss musicians who wore straitjackets: Alice Cooper, whom they saw in concert, and Johnny Rotten in the Sex Pistols' 'God Save the Queen' video.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck says he has nothing more to add, and the hosts close with the show's production credit and a note about where to listen.
